recipe.history:
The loaded, messy everything-in-the-fridge burger is perhaps the most American of all culinary expressions: a celebration of abundance, improvisation, and the deeply held belief that more is always better. Its most legitimate ancestor is the pulled pork sandwich of the American South, which traces its roots through the barbecue traditions of the Carolinas, Georgia, and Tennessee — traditions that themselves descend from the open-pit cooking practices that enslaved African Americans developed and practiced on Southern plantations, blending West African cooking techniques with the hog-centric agricultural economy of the antebellum South. Carolina pulled pork is defined by the long, slow cooking of pork shoulder over indirect heat or wood smoke until the collagen breaks down completely and the meat can be pulled apart into tender, smoky shreds; it is traditionally served with coleslaw — either vinegar-dressed in the Eastern Carolina style or mayonnaise-based in the Lexington style — and with pickles, whose acidity cuts through the fat of the pork. The hot sauce tradition that runs alongside all of this barbecue culture traces its own history through Louisiana hot sauces, Caribbean pepper sauces, and the tabletop condiment culture of Southern diners.

The concept of the loaded burger — pulled pork and coleslaw piled on top of a beef patty — became a fixture of American gastropub menus in the early 2000s and 2010s, when the gastropub movement was exploring ways to combine the informality of pub food with the ambition of restaurant-quality ingredients and techniques. The combination of beef and pork on a single bun — sometimes called the 'meat on meat' burger by the irreverent cooks who pioneered it — is an act of deliberate excess that nonetheless has an internal logic: the pulled pork adds a smoky, tender, slightly sweet register that beef alone cannot provide, the coleslaw adds freshness and crunch, and the pickles and hot sauce add the acid that keeps the whole construction from collapsing into a single undifferentiated mass of richness. The Fight at the Not Okay Chore-ral Burger embraces this tradition without apology.

I have strong opinions about coleslaw, which is unusual for someone with my general kitchen philosophy of equanimity, but coleslaw is a deeply personal subject. My family made Eastern Carolina-style vinegar slaw — no mayonnaise, just apple cider vinegar, celery seed, sugar, salt, and shaved cabbage — and I ate it my entire childhood as the counterpoint to pulled pork, and that combination of textures and flavors was written into me at such an early age that no other coleslaw has ever fully satisfied me. The first time I put that slaw on a burger — on a night when I had leftover pulled pork and a patty in the fridge and no particular plan — I understood intuitively that this was a complete meal, that the combination of beef and pork and the bright acid of the slaw was not a compromise or a shortcut but an actual thing, a composed dish that happened to be stacked vertically between two halves of a bun. I have made it deliberately ever since.

Of all the burgers in this collection, the Fight at the Not Okay Chore-ral Burger presents perhaps the most vivid argument for medium rare cooking: it is a burger of layers, and those layers must have structural integrity. A medium-rare patty at 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit provides the yielding but firm foundation that allows the pulled pork, coleslaw, pickles, and hot sauce to pile on top without the whole construction collapsing into chaos. A well-done patty — compressed, dry, dense — would be both unpleasant to eat and structurally insufficient: the weight of the toppings would press it into the bun without resistance. Medium rare provides the give, the juice, the presence. It is the load-bearing element in a deliberately overloaded structure, and without it, everything above it is just a mess. With it, everything above it is a meal.
ingredients: 1 large egg beaten with 1 tbsp water, for egg wash
For the pulled pork (start the day before or 8 to 10 hours ahead):
1/2 head green cabbage (about 600g), very thinly shaved
your preferred hot sauce (Crystal, Texas Pete, or Tabasco)
softened unsalted butter, for toasting buns
instructions: 1. Make the pulled pork (8 to 10 hours ahead or overnight): Combine brown sugar, smoked paprika, garlic powder, onion powder, cumin, black pepper, salt, dried mustard, and cayenne in a bowl. Rub the entire pork shoulder with this mixture, coating thoroughly. Place in a slow cooker or Dutch oven.

2. In a small bowl, whisk apple cider vinegar, ketchup, brown sugar (for sauce), Worcestershire, and hot sauce. Pour over the pork. Cook low and slow: in a slow cooker on LOW for 8 to 10 hours, or in a 275°F (135°C) oven in a covered Dutch oven for 6 to 8 hours, until the pork shreds effortlessly with two forks.
3. Remove the pork and shred completely with two forks. Skim the fat from the cooking liquid and return enough liquid to the pork to keep it moist and saucy. Taste and adjust seasoning. Keep warm.

4. Make the buns: Combine flour, yeast, sugar, and salt in the stand mixer bowl with dough hook. Add warm milk, water, and egg. Mix, then add butter gradually. Knead on medium-high until smooth, 8 minutes. Rise until doubled, 1 to 1.5 hours. Divide into 6 portions, shape, proof 40 minutes. Preheat oven to 375°F (190°C). Egg wash, sesame seeds, bake 18 to 20 minutes. Cool.

5. Make the vinegar coleslaw: In a small saucepan, combine apple cider vinegar, sugar, celery seeds, salt, and pepper. Heat over low heat, stirring until sugar and salt dissolve. Cool completely. In a large bowl, combine shaved cabbage and grated carrot. Pour the cooled dressing over the vegetables and toss well. Let sit for at least 30 minutes, tossing occasionally. The slaw should be tangy, crunchy, and bright. Drain excess liquid before using.
6. Make the burger sauce: Whisk mayonnaise, yellow mustard, hot sauce, apple cider vinegar, and brown sugar together until smooth. Refrigerate until needed.

7. Form the patties: Divide beef into 6 portions (about 150g each). Shape into 4-inch patties, 3/4 inch thick, with a center dimple. Season generously with kosher salt and black pepper just before cooking.

8. Cook the patties: Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat until smoking. Cook patties undisturbed for 3 minutes on the first side. Flip and immediately lay 2 slices of American cheese on each patty. Cook 2 to 2.5 more minutes. Add a splash of water and cover to steam-melt the cheese for 30 seconds. The internal temperature must reach 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C) — medium rare, the only correct temperature. Rest patties on a rack for 3 minutes.
9. Toast the buns: Butter the cut sides and toast in the skillet butter-side down over medium heat until golden, about 1 minute.

10. Assemble — embrace the mess: Spread burger sauce generously on both bun halves. Place the double-cheese-covered patty on the bottom bun. Pile 6 to 8 pickle chips on top of the cheese. Pile a generous handful of vinegar coleslaw on top of the pickles. Pile a generous heap of warm pulled pork on top of the slaw. Shake 4 to 5 dashes of hot sauce over everything. Cap with the top bun and press down firmly. Eat immediately over a plate, because this burger will fight back.
